featured.description: A small collection of recent experiments, enterprise migrations, and side-quests.

efengine.title: EFENGINE — C++ Game Engine
efengine.desc: A from-scratch 3D engine in C++17 on OpenGL 4.5 Core — PBR with split-sum IBL, shadow mapping, an HDR post chain, a versioned binary scene format and a docked ImGui editor, all under RAII rules with no exceptions.
efengine.description:
EFENGINE is my most ambitious project: a 3D engine written from scratch in C++17 on OpenGL 4.5 Core. It renders PBR materials lit by point and directional lights with full image-based lighting — diffuse irradiance plus split-sum specular, both precomputed by compute shaders — over shadow mapping, a skybox and an HDR post chain of bloom, tonemap and FXAA. Scenes live in a node graph addressed by generational handles and persist to .efe, a chunked, versioned binary format of my own with a reader hostile to corrupt input. On top sits a docked ImGui editor: hierarchy, inspector, live material editing and scene save/load.

What holds it together is a set of non-negotiable rules. Every gl* call is confined to efecom, the RHI layer — the renderer never sees OpenGL. No raw new/delete and no exceptions: ownership is a value or a unique_ptr, programmer errors trip an assert, recoverable failures come back as return values, and every subsystem is RAII — constructing it brings it up, destroying it tears it down.

phases.label: Fase 0
phases.title: Foundations
phases.desc: CMake with FetchContent, GLFW/GLAD/GLM, Log and Assert, Window and Application under end-to-end RAII, doctest on CTest. Closes with the first triangle on screen.

phases.label: Fase 1
phases.title: Core rendering
phases.desc: Shader, Texture via stb_image, Material, vertex layouts and Mesh; a camera with orbit, pan and zoom. Shaders move to being loaded from disk.

phases.label: Fase 2
phases.title: Scene and lights
phases.desc: Time, a ResourceManager cached by key, a Renderer with BeginScene/Submit, point lights, framebuffers and the first ImGui debug UI.

phases.label: Fase 3
phases.title: HDR and post-processing
phases.desc: Exposure on the camera, TonemapPass as the first IPostPass, and bloom and FXAA chained by ping-pong between two scratch framebuffers.

phases.label: Fase 4
phases.title: OpenGL 4.5 and the RHI
phases.desc: The jump to 4.5 Core with DSA and shaders at #version 450. efecom is born: no gl* call lives outside the RHI. Skybox and directional shadow mapping.

phases.label: Fase 5
phases.title: Graph, .efe and editor
phases.desc: SceneGraph by generational handles, per-node behaviors, and the .efe binary format — chunked, versioned, with a reader hostile to corrupt files. The sandbox becomes a docked editor.

phases.label: Fase 6
phases.title: Full IBL
phases.desc: Diffuse irradiance plus split-sum specular: GGX prefiltering at one dispatch per mip and a BRDF LUT, both by compute shader. Emission maps and normal strength land too.

systems.label: efecom · RHI
systems.role: The only surface that talks to the GPU. Opaque u32 handles, zero OpenGL types in the API, a replaceable GL 4.5 backend. It does not depend on efengine.

systems.label: renderer
systems.role: PBR with point and directional lights, diffuse and specular IBL, the shadow pass, the skybox and the PostChain of bloom, tonemap and FXAA.

systems.label: scene
systems.role: A node graph keyed by handle + generation: destroying a node invalidates its old handles. Hierarchical transforms that only recompute what is dirty, and per-node behaviors.

systems.label: resources
systems.role: Owner of everything that arrives from disk by path: shaders, textures with an explicit color space, and FBX models via Assimp. Caches and hands back observer pointers.

systems.label: serialization
systems.role: The .efe format: a versioned header and FourCC chunks. A single Serialize(Ar&) per type serves both reading and writing; unknown chunks are skipped by size.

systems.label: sandbox
systems.role: A docked Unity-style ImGui editor: hierarchy, inspector, live materials, a render panel, frame stats and scene save/load.

bancoProvincia.title: Provincia Casa Financiera — Core Services Migration
bancoProvincia.desc: Lifting the legacy Axis2 / Java 8 web services of Banco de la Provincia de Buenos Aires' Uruguayan branch onto Spring Boot 3 and Java 17 — 7 repositories, ~4,600 classes — with connectivity rewired from JNDI to a managed MSSQL DataSource.
bancoProvincia.role: Backend — legacy SOAP/WSDL services onto Spring Boot, team of 3
bancoProvincia.description: Long-running modernization of the legacy Axis2 SOAP services behind core banking at Provincia Casa Financiera, the Uruguayan branch of Banco de la Provincia de Buenos Aires. I own the backend: taking the legacy SOAP/WSDL services onto Java 17 + Spring Boot 3, replacing JNDI-bound resources with a managed MSSQL DataSource, and untangling years of tightly-coupled service contracts without breaking downstream consumers. In parallel a colleague split the Struts frontend and its consumer layer into two applications — a new Angular frontend and a backend-for-frontend that reaches the migrated services over either SOAP or REST, switchable at runtime if one path degrades.

modules.role: SOAP→REST dispatcher with dual XML/JSON responses.

modules.label: Service Plugins
modules.role: Per-service business logic loaded by the dispatcher.

modules.label: Messaging & Transaction Format
modules.role: Banking message contracts and transaction formatting.

modules.label: Web Tier — Core
modules.role: The presentation tier — the platform's largest surface.

modules.label: Web Tier — Services
modules.role: Service-client layer between the web tier and backend.

phases.title: Discovery & indexing
phases.desc: Index all seven repositories into a knowledge graph to map the real service and call surface.

phases.title: Service-by-service migration
phases.desc: Lift modules onto Spring Boot 3 and Java 17, rewire JNDI to a managed MSSQL DataSource, and preserve SOAP contracts via dual XML/JSON.

phases.title: Contract testing
phases.desc: OpenAPI (Swagger) definitions with Schemathesis property and fuzz testing to guarantee parity with the legacy services.

phases.title: Cutover
phases.desc: Module by module — Core Services and Security are live on Spring Boot 3; the rest are in flight.

bbva.title: BBVA — API Migration & Test Coverage
bbva.desc: Took test coverage on new endpoints from 20% to 85%+ across ~48 APIs, inside a 10-engineer team, with every deployment gated through Jenkins, OpenShift and SonarQube.
bbva.role: Test engineering and pre-migration work, team of 10
bbva.description: Engaged on BBVA's internal platform to migrate API services to Spring Boot and stand up disciplined test coverage across the surface. I took coverage on new endpoints from 20% to 85%+ across ~48 APIs using JUnit 5 and Mockito, in a team of 10, with deployments gated through Jenkins, OpenShift and SonarQube. The point wasn't the coverage number — it was making a codebase nobody trusted safe to change.

mobileBanking.title: Winterbotham — Mobile Banking App
mobileBanking.desc: A cross-platform mobile banking app in React Native + Expo, shipped to iOS and Android by a team of four — with WebAuthn authentication and a backend-for-frontend carrying the integration logic.
mobileBanking.role: Frontend, plus the backend-for-frontend and WebAuthn integration
mobileBanking.description: A mobile banking application for Winterbotham, built in React Native + Expo by a team of four over 18 months. My main surface was the frontend, and it extended into a backend-for-frontend carrying the connection logic to the core backend another firm was building in parallel. I also integrated WebAuthn while it was still an emerging standard with thin documentation — the part where a mistake becomes a security incident rather than a bug.

voxel.title: Minecraft-like Terrain Generation
voxel.desc: Three Voxel World Generation using Perlin noise algorithm in Three.js with 3D First Person Controller
voxel.description:
A sophisticated 3D voxel world renderer with procedural terrain generation, chunk streaming, and first-person controls. Built with Three.js and Next.js.
            Procedural Terrain Generation: Uses Perlin noise for realistic terrain and cave systems
            Infinite World Streaming: Dynamic chunk loading/unloading based on camera position
            First-Person Controls: WASD movement with mouse look and pointer lock
            Optimized Rendering: Instanced rendering for high performance
            Configurable World: Customizable chunk size, terrain parameters, and block types
            Caching System: Server-side chunk caching with deterministic generation

biome.title: Biome Terrain Engine
biome.description:
The generator produces biome maps at heightmap resolutions compatible with Unity Terrain (up to 513×513), using optimized two-dimensional data structures to represent both biome distribution and their gradual intensities. The system includes HSV color visualization for debugging and analysis, allowing for the rapid identification of transition zones between biomes.

Key features:

Weighted biome distribution using configurable seed points
Organic propagation algorithm with customizable decay rates
Support for multiple biomes with varying intensities
Generation of intensity maps for smooth transitions
Native integration with Unity Terrain System
Automatic export of biome maps as PNG textures

Ideal for projects requiring procedurally generated worlds with realistic ecosystems and natural transitions between different terrain types.

hackflix.title: Hackflix
hackflix.desc: Browse for the latest movies easily.
hackflix.description: A web-based movie catalog platform that replicates the user experience of modern streaming services, developed entirely with React and vanilla CSS without any dependencies on styling frameworks. The project demonstrates mastery of reusable component architecture and advanced CSS techniques to achieve a polished and responsive interface. The application implements a modular component system that includes horizontal carousels, movie cards with hover effects, dynamic navigation, and adaptive layouts that maintain visual consistency across multiple devices and screen resolutions. All styling is managed using pure CSS with modern methodologies such as Flexbox and CSS Grid.

truqui.title: Truqui
truqui.desc: A Progressive Web App (PWA) specializing in digital scorekeeping for Truco, the most popular traditional card game in Uruguay and Argentina. Designed to work completely offline, it allows players to keep accurate and efficient score tracking without relying on an internet connection. The app leverages modern PWA capabilities to deliver a native cross-platform experience, installable directly from the browser on mobile devices, tablets, and desktops. Its offline-first architecture guarantees full availability through Service Workers and local storage, ensuring that games are never interrupted by connectivity issues.

agents.intro: On codebases too large to hold in one head, an agent is only as sharp as the ground truth you give it. My method keeps AI anchored to real structure and provable contracts — every answer traced through a graph, every endpoint checked against its spec.

pillars.principle: Traverse the graph — don't grep it
pillars.title: Project indexing
pillars.body: I index each codebase into a knowledge graph of functions, routes, call chains and service contracts. Agents traverse how the code actually connects instead of grepping or guessing through semantic search — so a sprawling migration surface answers to a query, not a full-text scan.

pillars.principle: The spec is the test suite
pillars.title: Schemathesis + OpenAPI
pillars.body: Schemathesis reads a service's OpenAPI schema and generates property-based tests — hundreds of boundary, malformed and stateful cases the contract implies but nobody writes by hand. It surfaces schema drift and unexpected 500s before a client ever sees them — exactly what a migrated endpoint has to prove.

pillars.title: API test harness
pillars.body: I wrapped that flow into a small app: point it at any service exposing an OpenAPI schema and it runs the full Schemathesis suite, surfaces failures and reports contract coverage. Testing a new microservice becomes configuration, not a fresh test project.
